title: Theatre infection control: standard and additional precautions
audience: Operating-theatre staff, theatre cleaning contractors and the co-ordinators who supervise them. Cleaning contractors apply the cleaning and waste steps only; surgical technique is for theatre clinicians.
learningOutcomes: Distinguish standard precautions, which apply to every patient, from additional precautions that depend on how an infection travels.
Explain why the theatre applies the same baseline to every patient, including patients with a blood-borne virus.
Identify who in the theatre is responsible for checking standards and how the check is recorded.

instruction.heading: Two layers of precaution
instruction.body: Infection control in a theatre rests on two layers. The first is the baseline that applies to every patient at all times, whatever the diagnosis. Its contents are hand cleaning, protective items for any contact with blood or other body fluids, careful handling of patient equipment and linen, avoiding sharps injuries, cleaning of the environment and dealing with spills, and careful waste handling. The second layer is added where a particular route of spread needs it: airborne, droplet or contact precautions. The second layer always sits on top of the first and never replaces it.

instruction.heading: Why the baseline treats all fluid as a risk
instruction.body: The operating-theatre paper regards every sample of blood, every blood product and all other body fluids as a possible carrier of infection, whatever the diagnosis, and however risky a case looks. It identifies two main workplace routes for HIV and hepatitis B: needles and blades carrying blood or other body fluids that pierce the skin, and splashes that land on the eyes, on damaged skin or in a wound. Blocking those routes means avoiding sharps injuries and placing a physical barrier between workers and every source of blood or other body fluids. The learner guide reaches the same conclusion through its standard precautions and its sharps rules (see “Body fluid exposure: first response and reporting” and “Sharps: handling, containers and injury response”).

instruction.heading: Additional precautions and the size figures
instruction.body: Beyond the baseline, the same document also lists extra measures for three routes, and gives size figures for two of them. The learner guide gives no size figures for those routes. The additional measures for a particular case come from the theatre infection-control plan that the clinical team sets. The learner guide lists possible measures such as isolation, special ventilation, enhanced cleaning and extra protective items (see “Enhanced cleaning under added controls for infection spread” and “Terminal cleaning after transmission-based precautions”).

instruction.heading: Terminology and blood-borne virus patients
instruction.body: The theatre document uses the term universal precautions for the baseline. The learner guide uses standard precautions, and it governs where the two differ, so this lesson uses standard precautions for the same principle. According to the same paper, a person living with hepatitis B, hepatitis C or HIV receives the same care as anybody else, under the baseline. The learner guide adds a confidentiality rule: a person condition is not disclosed to others, and any extra measure is carried out discreetly. Taken together, the rules mean the same care for everyone, with no disclosure.

instruction.heading: Who checks the standard
instruction.body: Responsibility for following the standards rests with every person working in theatre or in a clinical role. Co-ordinators must confirm that cleanliness expectations are satisfied, and take corrective steps when they are not. It makes theatre operational managers responsible for regular audits, with a written record. The learner guide places the duty to write policies and train workers on the employer, and places the duty to follow them and report breaches on each worker. The facility written role descriptions decide who does what in practice.

instruction.heading: Jurisdiction and references
instruction.body: The theatre document is undated and unattributed, and it contains UK-style references such as a trust waste policy. Its jurisdiction is unknown, so it is treated here as practice content only. UK-only policy references do not apply in Australia. State and territory law and the facility policy govern waste, reporting and the theatre plan.

procedure: Open the theatre written policy on infection prevention and note each baseline measure it asks for in every case.
Check the additional-precaution plan for the current patient, if the clinical team has set one.
Confirm with the co-ordinator which protective items and cleaning steps apply to the task.
Report any gap between the written policy and what happens in the theatre to the co-ordinator.
Record the standard checked and the outcome on the theatre checklist.

workedExamples.situation: During a list, a theatre nurse asks a cleaner why a gown and gloves are needed to wipe the table between two cases, when the second patient infection status is not known.
workedExamples.reasoning: The table may carry blood or other body fluid from any patient. The baseline applies to every patient, so the protection is needed whatever the diagnosis. Additional precautions would apply only if the theatre plan for that patient adds them.

workedExamples.situation: Two staff members in a corridor discuss whether a patient in the next room has a blood-borne virus.
workedExamples.reasoning: Stop the discussion. The patient receives the same care as anyone else, and the information is confidential. Raise the concern with the co-ordinator, and do not repeat what was said.

equipmentAndPpe: Theatre policy document and the case plan
Protective items for the baseline, as set by the theatre

commonErrors.error: Applying precautions only to patients with a known infection.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the baseline for every patient, every time.

commonErrors.error: Treating the size figures in the theatre document as an Australian rule.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the case plan and the learner guide.

commonErrors.error: Discussing a patient virus status where others can hear.
commonErrors.prevention: Keep the information to those who need it for care, and report any breach to the co-ordinator.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: The theatre document is undated and unattributed, and it includes UK-style references. Its jurisdiction is unknown. Check state and territory requirements and the facility policy before relying on any point.
They are not adopted in this lesson.

Cleaning contractors must not apply the surgical technique in “Sharps and instruments in theatre” to “Theatre skin preparation, hand decontamination and who checks the standard” to their own work. Follow the theatre guidance for the cleaning task.
Completing this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to perform regulated work.

qualityStandard: Learner states the two layers of precaution and gives one example of each.
Learner explains why every blood or other body fluid is treated as a risk, whatever the diagnosis.
Learner names the person accountable for checking theatre standards and how the check is recorded.
documentationEvidence: Theatre checklist entry recording the baseline checked and the outcome.
Notification to the co-ordinator of any gap, with the time and the response.
summary: The baseline applies to every patient, and additional precautions are layered on top of it.
The same care applies to a patient with a blood-borne virus, with no disclosure to others.
Co-ordinators ensure standards are met, and operational managers audit and record them.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which statement describes standard precautions in the theatre?
options: They apply only to patients with a known infection today
They apply to every patient at all times, whatever the diagnosis
They apply only when a visitor enters the theatre in the morning
They apply only in the recovery area and in the corridor outside

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is an additional, transmission-based route of spread?
A patient has hepatitis B. Which rule applies in the theatre?
options: Treat them differently and mark the file where others can see it and tell the whole team
Treat them the same as any patient, with the baseline precautions, and keep the information confidential
Refuse to clean the theatre after their case and leave the room closed until the next day
Use double the usual amount of cleaning product and leave it on the surfaces overnight

Conflict and resolution: the theatre document uses universal precautions; the learner guide, the official Australian source, uses standard precautions and governs. The theatre size figures for airborne and droplet spread conflict with the learner guide, which gives none; the learner guide governs and the figures are not used (UNCONFIRMED).
UNCONFIRMED: airborne and droplet size figures, not checked against any Australian source.
